title: My Father works (John 5:10–30)
hookLine: healing on the sabbath: my Father is working still, and so am I
last: DO YOU WANT TO BE WELL?

cards: A man walks through Jerusalem with his rolled-up mat under his arm. It's the sabbath, the day of rest that Jewish law protects, and some of the religious leaders stop him: it is not lawful to carry your bed today.
His answer is wonderfully human: the man who healed me told me to. Who was it? He doesn't know.
He never got the name; Jesus had slipped away into the crowd. Later Jesus finds him in the temple, and the question of the sabbath reaches Jesus himself.

teach.b: Jesus tells him: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee." The man goes and tells the leaders who healed him, and the argument begins.

teach.h: A DEBATE AMONG JEWS ABOUT REST.
teach.b: Remember, this is a debate among Jews about what keeping the sabbath means. Jesus answers in one sentence: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work." Hitherto means until now.
Genesis says God rested on the seventh day.

teach.h: GOD STILL HOLDS UP THE WORLD.
teach.b: Yet the world keeps going on the sabbath: babies are born, rain falls, hearts beat. Jewish teachers asked the same question: how can God rest, when the world needs holding up every moment?

Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of that time, answered that God never stops making and sustaining the world. Jesus stands inside that thought: if the Father is still at work, the Son works with him.

His listeners hear the claim clearly: he is calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Then he describes how it works between them: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do."
Like an apprentice at a workbench, watching the master's hands and copying them.

teach.h: MY FATHER WORKETH HITHERTO, AND I WORK.
teach.b: In Christian teaching, this passage is a key to who Jesus is: not a rival to God, but the Son doing what the Father does.
And in Jesus's words it's a picture of a God who doesn't clock out, still at the work of healing and giving life.

how: Christians read this passage as a teaching about Jesus as the Son of God; some also see in it a call to join in God's ongoing work of healing and care.

games.q: you're the healed man, stopped in the street for carrying your mat on the sabbath. what do you say?
o: the man who healed me told me to carry it.
games.why: he says the man who healed him told him to, but he doesn't even know his name. Jesus finds him later in the temple.

practice: Notice what's working in you right now without any effort: your heart beating, your lungs filling, the ground holding you up.
Then picture one small good work you could do, a message to someone lonely, a repair you've put off, carrying something for someone.
If you pray, ask to see where God is already at work, and join in; if you don't, choose the work anyway.
